Here is the itemized breakdown of the key scholars and works cited, relied upon, or disputed by James W. Aageson across the twelve B001 comparisons in his doctoral dissertation (Paul's Use of Scripture, Oxford University, 1983).
1. B001-1: Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6
E. Earle Ellis, Paul's Use of the Old Testament (1957), pp. 16–17, 82–84.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for categorizing double citations in Paul. Ellis demonstrates that minor variations like the transposition of ἐπίστευσεν and Ἀβραάμ between Rom 4:3 and Gal 3:6 do not alter the semantic sense but reflect Paul's minor quotational inconsistency.
C.E.B. Cranfield, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, Vol. I (1975), pp. 226ff.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for exegetical analysis of Romans 4. Cranfield shows how Paul isolates the chronological sequence of Genesis 15:6 (faith reckoned as righteousness) prior to Genesis 17 (circumcision) to argue that Gentile justification is independent of the law.
Ernst Käsemann, "The Faith of Abraham in Romans 4" in Perspectives on Paul (1971), pp. 79–101.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to demonstrate that Paul’s use of Genesis 15:6 extracts a theological principle of faith-righteousness vs. works-righteousness that runs counter to traditional Tannaitic interpretations of Abraham’s merit.
2. B001-2: Romans 9:25 / Hosea 2:23 (LXX 2:25)
Dietrich-Alex Koch, Die Schrift als Zeuge des Evangeliums (1980) / "Beobachtungen zum christologischen Schriftgebrauch..." (1980), pp. 174–191.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for text-critical alignment. Koch notes that Paul follows LXX-B (ἀγαπήσω / ἠγαπημένην) rather than LXX-A (ἐλεήσω / ἠλεημένην), illustrating Paul's reliance on specific Greek manuscript branches.
E. Earle Ellis, Paul's Use of the Old Testament (1957), pp. 81, 140.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to explain textual substitution. Ellis shows that Paul replaced ἐρῶ with καλέσω to create a deliberate verbal catchword link (gezerah shawah) with κληθήσονται in Hosea 1:10 and ἐκάλεσεν in Romans 9:24.
C.H. Dodd, According to the Scriptures (1952), pp. 41–43.
Role / Relevance: Cited regarding the early Christian testimonia tradition, where Hosea 2:23 and 1:10 were clustered as prophetic proofs for the calling of the Gentiles.
3. B001-3: Romans 9:26 / Hosea 1:10 (LXX 2:1)
Dietrich-Alex Koch, Die Schrift als Zeuge des Evangeliums (1980).
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to establish that Romans 9:26 aligns verbatim with Codex Alexandrinus (LXX-A), which includes ἐκεῖ and omits καὶ αὐτοί.
Barnabas Lindars, New Testament Apologetic (1961), pp. 37–38, 244–245.
Role / Relevance: Cited for the early church's apologetic application of Hosea 1:10 to Gentile converts as "sons of the living God."
4. B001-4: Romans 10:11 / Isaiah 28:16
C.H. Dodd, According to the Scriptures (1952), pp. 41–43, and Rendel Harris, Testimonies, 2 vols. (1916, 1920).
Role / Relevance: Relied upon regarding the composite "stone" text (combining Isa 28:16 and Isa 8:14 in Rom 9:33 and 10:11). Dodd and Harris argue for a pre-Pauline Christian florilegium/testimony collection.
C.K. Barrett, "Romans 9:30-10:21: Fall and Responsibility of Israel" (1982), pp. 139–144.
Role / Relevance: Disputed in part. Barrett argues that the "stone of stumbling" in Rom 9:32–33 / 10:11 refers primarily to the Law; Aageson argues alongside Cranfield that Paul intended the stone to refer christologically to Jesus.
C.E.B. Cranfield, "Some Notes on Romans 9:30-33" (1975), pp. 35–43.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to explain why Paul inserted πᾶς in Rom 10:11 (Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων...) after omitting it in Rom 9:33—namely, due to verbal catchword influence from Joel 2:32 (πᾶς) in Rom 10:13.
5. B001-5: Romans 10:13 / Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5)
Barnabas Lindars, New Testament Apologetic (1961), pp. 37–38.
Role / Relevance: Cited for comparative usage. Lindars notes that while Luke in Acts 2:21 uses Joel 2:32 as an eschatological prophecy of the Spirit at Pentecost, Paul isolates πᾶς and ἐπικαλέω as exegetical catchwords to prove universal salvation for both Jews and Greeks.
C.E.B. Cranfield, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, Vol. II (1979), pp. 531ff.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for exegesis of ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου, showing how Paul applies the divine Old Testament title Kyrios directly to the risen Jesus.
6. B001-6: Romans 11:34 / Isaiah 40:13
E. Earle Ellis, Paul's Use of the Old Testament (1957), p. 13, 69.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to establish that Paul’s word order σύμβουλος αὐτοῦ in both Rom 11:34 and 1 Cor 2:16 follows LXX-A against LXX-B (αὐτοῦ σύμβουλος), and to show how Paul quotes different clauses of the same verse in different letters.
7. B001-7: Romans 15:12 / Isaiah 11:10
Dietrich-Alex Koch, "Beobachtungen zum christologischen Schriftgebrauch..." (1980), pp. 174–191.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for identifying Isa 11:10 as part of a pre-Pauline christological catena utilized in early Gentile mission contexts.
C.E.B. Cranfield, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, Vol. II (1979), pp. 750ff.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to explain the midrashic stringing technique (charaz) in Rom 15:9–12, where four passages are chained together via the catchword ἔθνη.
8. B001-8: 1 Corinthians 1:19 / Isaiah 29:14
E. Earle Ellis, "Exegetical Patterns in I Corinthians and Romans" in Prophecy and Hermeneutic in Early Christianity (1978), pp. 213–220.
Role / Relevance: Discussed extensively. Ellis proposes that 1 Cor 1:18–31 was an independent Jewish-Christian midrashic unit adopted by Paul; Aageson notes that even if pre-Pauline, Isa 29:14 functions as the active verbal and thematic generator of Paul's discourse on divine wisdom vs. worldly foolishness.
Hans Conzelmann, 1 Corinthians (1975), pp. 48ff.
Role / Relevance: Cited for textual and structural analysis of Paul’s replacement of LXX κρύψω with ἀθετήσω in 1 Cor 1:19.
9. B001-9: 1 Corinthians 6:16 / Genesis 2:24
E. Earle Ellis, Paul's Use of the Old Testament (1957), pp. 70–71, 83–84.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for double-citation analysis, comparing 1 Cor 6:16 with Eph 5:31 to prove that insertion of γάρ, φησίν in 1 Cor 6:16 was purely for epistolary sentence integration.
David Daube, The New Testament and Rabbinic Judaism (1956), pp. 67ff.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for hermeneutical background on how 1st-century Jewish exegesis frequently transformed narrative creation accounts (haggadah) into normative behavioral rules (halakah).
10. B001-10: 1 Corinthians 9:9 / Deuteronomy 25:4
A.E. Harvey, "'The Workman is Worthy of His Hire': Fortunes of a Proverb in the Early Church," Novum Testamentum 24 (1982), pp. 209–221.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to contextualize Paul's use of Deut 25:4 ("you shall not muzzle an ox") within early Christian debates over an apostle's right to financial support.
G.M. Lee, "Studies in Texts: I Cor. 9:9-10," Theology 71 (1968), pp. 122–123.
Role / Relevance: Cited for the lexical variant κημώσεις (printed in 1 Cor 9:9 in place of LXX φιμώσεις).
Joseph Bonsirven, Exégèse rabbinique et exégèse paulinienne (1939), pp. 88ff.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon for identifying Paul’s use of Hillel’s first rule (qal wahomer / a fortiori reasoning: if God cares for oxen, how much more for human ministers).
11. B001-11: 1 Corinthians 10:7 / Exodus 32:6
Wayne Meeks, "'And Rose Up to Play': Midrash and Paraenesis in I Corinthians 10:1-22," Journal for the Study of the New Testament 16 (1982), pp. 64–78.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to show that 1 Cor 10:1–13 is a midrashic parenesis where Israel's wilderness story (Exod 32:6) functions as an ethical warning against idolatry and pagan meals.
Leonhard Goppelt, Typos: The Typological Interpretation of the Old Testament in the New (1939; Eng. trans. 1982), pp. 129–136, 223–225.
Role / Relevance: Disputed in part. Goppelt argues that 1 Cor 10:1–13 is salvation-historical typology; Aageson argues that τύπος here means a moral "warning" or "instructive example," not redemptive-historical typology.
12. B001-12: Galatians 3:13 / Deuteronomy 21:23
Hans Dieter Betz, Galatians: A Commentary on Paul's Letter to the Churches in Galatia (1979), pp. 148ff.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon regarding text modification in Gal 3:13. Betz and Aageson emphasize that the omission of ὑπὸ θεοῦ from LXX Deut 21:23 (κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ θεοῦ) was an intentional theological adjustment to avoid implying that Christ was accursed by God the Father.
Ernest De Witt Burton, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians (1921), pp. 168ff.
Role / Relevance: Cited for grammatical and text-critical analysis of Paul's citation formulas and omissions in Galatians 3–4.
E.P. Sanders, Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People (1983), pp. 21–23.
Role / Relevance: Relied upon to analyze the terminological character and midrashic structure of the curse catena in Galatians 3:6–14.
